Unit 1(a) · Propositional logic

Syllabus 1(a): propositional logic, well-formed formulae, truth tables, satisfiable / unsatisfiable / valid formulae, equivalence laws, converse, inverse and contrapositive, chain rule, modus ponens. In the paper: 2–3 one-mark items in Question 1 and a 2–3-mark truth-table question in Section A, every year.

ConceptPropositions, connectives and well-formed formulae

A proposition is a statement that is either true (1) or false (0), never both. A propositional variable (p, q, r) stands for one. A well-formed formula (wff) is built by the rules: every variable (and 0, 1) is a wff; if P and Q are wffs so are ~P, (P ∧ Q), (P ∨ Q), (P ⇒ Q) and (P ⇔ Q). An interpretation gives each variable a truth value; the truth table lists all 2n interpretations.

pq~pp ∧ qp ∨ qp ⇒ qp ⇔ q
0010011
0110110
1000100
1101111
  • Precedence (highest first): ~, ∧, ∨, ⇒, ⇔.
  • p ⇒ q is false in exactly one row: p true, q false. A false antecedent makes the implication true (“vacuously”).
  • p ⇔ q is true when p and q have the same value (it is XNOR).

Implication fails only as 1 ⇒ 0. Everything else follows from that.

ConceptTautology, contradiction, contingency; valid, satisfiable, unsatisfiable

TermMeaningExample
Tautology (valid)true in every rowp ∨ ~p (law of excluded middle)
Contradiction (unsatisfiable)false in every rowp ∧ ~p (law of contradiction)
Contingencytrue in some rows, false in othersp ⇒ q
Satisfiabletrue in at least one rowevery tautology and every contingency

Two formulae are equivalent (P ≡ Q) when they have identical truth-table columns, i.e. when P ⇔ Q is a tautology. An argument is valid when (premises) ⇒ conclusion is a tautology. ISC also asks “verify whether A = B is valid”, meaning: are the two columns identical?

Tautology = valid; contradiction = unsatisfiable; satisfiable = not a contradiction.

FormulaeEquivalence laws (syllabus list)

LawStatement
Commutativep ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p;   p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p
Associative(p ∧ q) ∧ r ≡ p ∧ (q ∧ r); same for ∨
Distributivep ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r);   p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r)
De Morgan~(p ∧ q) ≡ ~p ∨ ~q;   ~(p ∨ q) ≡ ~p ∧ ~q
Implicationp ⇒ q ≡ ~p ∨ q
Biconditionalp ⇔ q ≡ (p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ p)
Identityp ≡ p
Negation (double)~(~p) ≡ p
Excluded middlep ∨ ~p ≡ 1 (true)
Contradictionp ∧ ~p ≡ 0 (false)
Simplification (∨)p ∨ p ≡ p;   p ∨ 1 ≡ 1;   p ∨ 0 ≡ p;   p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p
Simplification (∧)p ∧ p ≡ p;   p ∧ 1 ≡ p;   p ∧ 0 ≡ 0;   p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p

Name the law at every step of a proof — the step marks are for the names.

ConceptConverse, inverse and contrapositive

NameFormEquivalent to
Statementp ⇒ qits contrapositive
Converseq ⇒ pthe inverse
Inverse~p ⇒ ~qthe converse
Contrapositive~q ⇒ ~pthe statement

Example: “If a figure is a square, then it is a rectangle.” Converse: If it is a rectangle, it is a square (false). Inverse: If it is not a square, it is not a rectangle (false). Contrapositive: If it is not a rectangle, it is not a square (true, like the statement).

Contrapositive: swap AND negate. Converse: swap only. Inverse: negate only.

ConceptRules of inference: modus ponens and the chain rule

RulePremisesConclusionAs a tautology
Modus ponensp ⇒ q, pq((p ⇒ q) ∧ p) ⇒ q
Modus tollensp ⇒ q, ~q~p((p ⇒ q) ∧ ~q) ⇒ ~p
Chain rule (hypothetical syllogism)p ⇒ q, q ⇒ rp ⇒ r((p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ r)) ⇒ (p ⇒ r)

A classic invalid pattern is affirming the consequent: from p ⇒ q and q you may not conclude p.

Modus ponens: if p then q; p; therefore q.

ConceptWord problems as wff

Give each simple statement a letter, then translate the connective words: “and, but” → ∧; “or” → ∨; “not” → ~; “if … then”, “implies” → ⇒; “p only if q” → p ⇒ q (and “p if q” → q ⇒ p); “if and only if” → ⇔.

s: it is sunny; h: it is a holiday; o: the shop opens. “If it is sunny and not a holiday then the shop opens” = (s ∧ ~h) ⇒ o. “The shop opens only if it is not a holiday” = o ⇒ ~h.

“p only if q” is p ⇒ q, not q ⇒ p.

Worked exampleContrapositive, converse and inverse in words

“If a product is eco-friendly, then pollution is reduced.” (Board 2026 Q1(ix) asked the contrapositive.)

Show working
  • Contrapositive: If pollution is not reduced, then the product is not eco-friendly.
  • Converse: If pollution is reduced, then the product is eco-friendly.
  • Inverse: If a product is not eco-friendly, then pollution is not reduced.

Trap Writing “If pollution is reduced, the product is eco-friendly” for the contrapositive — that is the converse.

Worked exampleAssertion–Reason on De Morgan

Assertion: ~(X ∨ Y) ≡ ~X ∧ ~Y. Reason: it follows from the commutative law. (Board 2025 Q1(ii) pattern.)

  • (a) Both true, Reason explains Assertion
  • (b) Both true, Reason does not explain
  • (c) Assertion true, Reason false
  • (d) Both false
Show working

Answer (c). The Assertion is De Morgan’s law (true); the commutative law only reorders operands and cannot produce it, so the Reason is false.

Recall sheetRecall sheet

  • p ⇒ q ≡ ~p ∨ q; false only for 1 ⇒ 0.
  • p ⇔ q ≡ (p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ p); true when p, q agree.
  • Tautology: all 1s. Contradiction: all 0s. Contingency: mixed. Satisfiable: at least one 1.
  • Contrapositive ~q ⇒ ~p ≡ statement; converse q ⇒ p ≡ inverse ~p ⇒ ~q.
  • Modus ponens [(p ⇒ q) ∧ p] ⇒ q; chain rule [(p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ r)] ⇒ (p ⇒ r) — both tautologies.
  • Validity question: build the table with intermediate columns, compare the two final columns, write VALID / INVALID in capitals.
  • Redundancy: ~x ∨ (x ∧ y) ≡ ~x ∨ y — the step that finishes most law proofs.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • A–R or MCQ on converse / inverse / contrapositive of a worded implication (7 of 9 boards; B25, B25I, S25 in a row).
  • VSA: write the contrapositive of an “if … then” sentence (B26 1(ix)).
  • Section A [2–3]: tautology / contradiction / contingency by truth table, or “verify whether valid” (8 of 9 boards).
  • Prove the chain rule or modus ponens by laws [3] (B26 3(ii); syllabus names both).
  • A–R on De Morgan / equivalence with a wrong-law reason (B25 1(ii), B26 1(iii)).

Unit 1(b, c) · Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps

Syllabus 1(b), 1(c): binary values, postulates, AND / OR / NOT, basic theorems (duality, idempotence, commutativity, associativity, distributivity, operations with 0 and 1, complements, absorption, involution), De Morgan, SOP and POS, minterms and maxterms, canonical and cardinal forms, Karnaugh maps up to four variables. The heaviest unit on the paper: about 20 of the 70 marks.

ConceptPostulates and the three basic operations

Boolean algebra works on the set {0, 1} with OR (+), AND (·) and NOT (′). Huntington’s postulates: closure (A + B, A · B are in {0,1}); identity A + 0 = A, A · 1 = A; commutativity; distributivity A(B + C) = AB + AC and A + BC = (A + B)(A + C); complement A + A′ = 1, A · A′ = 0. Every other law is proved from these.

ABA'A·BA+B
00100
01101
10001
11011

In Boolean algebra 1 + 1 = 1 and there is no subtraction or division.

FormulaeLaws of Boolean algebra (each OR form is the dual of the AND form)

LawOR formAND form (dual)
IdentityA+0 = AA·1 = A
Null (operations with 0 and 1)A+1 = 1A·0 = 0
IdempotenceA+A = AA·A = A
ComplementA+A′ = 1A·A′ = 0
Involution(A′)′ = A—
CommutativeA+B = B+AA·B = B·A
Associative(A+B)+C = A+(B+C)(A·B)·C = A·(B·C)
DistributiveA·(B+C) = A·B+A·CA+B·C = (A+B)·(A+C)
AbsorptionA+A·B = AA·(A+B) = A
RedundancyA+A′·B = A+BA·(A′+B) = A·B
De Morgan(A+B)′ = A′·B′(A·B)′ = A′+B′
ConsensusA·B+A′·C+B·C = A·B+A′·C(A+B)(A′+C)(B+C) = (A+B)(A′+C)

Every law comes in a dual pair; learn one and write the other by duality.

ConceptPrinciple of duality

The dual of a Boolean expression or equation is obtained by interchanging + with · and 0 with 1, leaving every variable and every complement as it is. If an equation is true, its dual is also true.

  • Dual of A + 0 = A is A · 1 = A.
  • Dual of (A′+B)·(1+B) = A′+B is A′·B + 0·B = A′·B.
  • Keep the brackets of the original grouping: dual of A + B·C is A·(B + C).

Duality: swap + with · and 0 with 1; do NOT complement the variables (that is complementing).

ConceptDe Morgan’s theorem and complementing an expression

(A + B)′ = A′·B′ and (A·B)′ = A′ + B′, extended to any number of variables. To complement an expression: take the dual and complement every literal — i.e. swap + and ·, swap 0 and 1, and prime / unprime each variable, keeping the grouping in brackets.

Complement = dual + complement every literal.

ConceptSOP, POS, minterms and maxterms; canonical and cardinal forms

  • SOP: a sum of product terms (A′B + BC). POS: a product of sum terms ((A + B)(B′ + C)).
  • Minterm: a product containing every variable once (primed or not); it is 1 for exactly one input. Write a variable plain for 1, primed for 0: A=1,B=0,C=1 → AB′C = m5.
  • Maxterm: a sum containing every variable once; it is 0 for exactly one input. Write plain for 0, primed for 1: A=1,B=0,C=1 → A′ + B + C′ = M5.
  • Mi = (mi)′. A function’s minterms and maxterms partition all 2n rows.
  • Canonical form writes every term out in full; cardinal (shorthand) form lists the numbers: F = Σ(1,3,6) or F = π(2,5,7).
A B CMintermMaxterm
0 0 0m0 = A′B′C′M0 = A+B+C
0 0 1m1 = A′B′CM1 = A+B+C′
0 1 0m2 = A′BC′M2 = A+B′+C
0 1 1m3 = A′BCM3 = A+B′+C′
1 0 0m4 = AB′C′M4 = A′+B+C
1 0 1m5 = AB′CM5 = A′+B+C′
1 1 0m6 = ABC′M6 = A′+B′+C
1 1 1m7 = ABCM7 = A′+B′+C′

Minterm: 1 → plain. Maxterm: 0 → plain. Same index for both.

ConceptKarnaugh maps: the rules

  • Rows and columns are in Gray code order 00, 01, 11, 10, so neighbouring cells differ in exactly one variable. The map wraps round: the left and right edges are adjacent, so are top and bottom, and the four corners form one quad.
  • Group 1s (SOP) or 0s (POS) in rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells. A pair drops 1 variable, a quad 2, an octet 3.
  • Use the largest groups and the fewest of them; every 1 must be covered; overlapping is allowed; a group that covers nothing new is redundant.
  • Read a group: keep the variables that stay constant across it. SOP: constant 1 → plain, 0 → primed. POS: constant 0 → plain, 1 → primed, written as a sum.
  • Label the POS map with sums (A+B, A+B′, A′+B′, A′+B) and put 0s in the maxterm cells.

Octet: 3 variables go; quad: 2; pair: 1. Gray order 00 01 11 10.

Worked exampleDual and complement

(a) Find the dual of (A′ + B)·(1 + B) = A′ + B (Specimen 2025 Q1(iii)). (b) Find the complement of A′·(B·C′ + B′·C) (Specimen 2025 Q1(i)).

Show working

(a) Swap + ↔ · and 1 → 0: A′·B + 0·B = A′·B.

(b) Complement: A + (B′ + C)·(B + C′) = A + B′C′ + BC.

Recall sheetRecall sheet

  • Duality: + ↔ ·, 0 ↔ 1, literals unchanged. Complement: dual + prime every literal.
  • Absorption A + AB = A; redundancy A + A′B = A + B; consensus AB + A′C + BC = AB + A′C.
  • Distributive (OR form) A + BC = (A + B)(A + C) — used in almost every POS proof.
  • Minterm: 1 → plain, product. Maxterm: 0 → plain, sum. Mi = mi′.
  • Σ list and π list of one function are complementary; together they list 0 .. 2n−1.
  • K-map: Gray order, wrap-around, largest groups first, octet drops 3 / quad 2 / pair 1.
  • POS map: headings are sums, cells hold 0, a constant 0 gives a plain literal.
  • NAND-only from SOP: two levels of NAND. NOR-only from POS: two levels of NOR. A single literal still needs an inverter gate.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q1: dual of an equation with 0/1 terms (9 of 9 boards); complement of a 2–3-term expression (9 of 9); name the law (8 of 9).
  • Q1: canonical form of a cardinal function Σ/π (B25, B25I, S25).
  • Section A: 4-input word problem → truth table → SOP or POS [5], then K-map + gates, often NAND- or NOR-only [5] (every board).
  • Section A: a standalone 4-variable K-map, Σ with NAND-only or π with an octet [4 + 1] (every paper).
  • Simplify / prove with Boolean laws naming each law [2–3]; minterm and maxterm for given values [1 + 1].

Unit 2 · Computer hardware: gates, adders, encoders, decoders, multiplexers

Syllabus 2: elementary logic gates, their use in circuits; half and full adders, majority circuit, encoders, decoders, multiplexers; NAND and NOR as universal gates. About 7 of the Section A marks: one 5-mark encoder / decoder / MUX block and a small adder or universal-gate block each year.

ConceptThe seven elementary gates

ABANDORNANDNORXORXNOR
00001101
01011010
10011010
11110001
  • XOR (A ⊕ B = A′B + AB′) is 1 when the inputs differ; for many inputs, when an odd number are 1.
  • XNOR (A ⊙ B = AB + A′B′) is 1 when the inputs are equal; it is the complement of XOR.
  • A bubble on a symbol means NOT: NAND = AND + bubble, NOR = OR + bubble.

Two NOR gates in series (second with both inputs tied) give OR; two NANDs give AND.

ConceptNAND and NOR are universal gates

A gate is universal if NOT, AND and OR — hence any Boolean function — can be built from it alone.

BuildNAND onlyNOR only
NOT A(A·A)′ = A′(A+A)′ = A′
A AND B((A·B)′)′ = A·B(A′+B′)′ = A·B (invert inputs first)
A OR B(A′·B′)′ = A+B (invert inputs first)((A+B)′)′ = A+B
XOR4 NAND gates5 NOR gates

Write the expression at the output of every gate — those labels carry the marks.

ConceptHalf adder and full adder

A half adder adds two bits: SUM = A ⊕ B, CARRY = A·B (1 XOR + 1 AND). A full adder adds three bits (two bits and the carry in): SUM = A ⊕ B ⊕ C, CARRY = AB + BC + CA. It is made from two half adders and an OR gate — 2 XOR, 2 AND, 1 OR.

ABSUMCARRY
0000
0110
1010
1101
ABCSUMCARRY
00000
00110
01010
01101
10010
10101
11001
11111

Build-up. The first half adder adds A and B (sum s1, carry c1); the second adds C to s1 (sum SUM, carry c2); a carry out occurs if either half adder carries, so CARRY = c1 + c2.

Half adder: 2 inputs, no carry in. Full adder: 3 inputs. Canonical: SUM = Σ(1,2,4,7), CARRY = Σ(3,5,6,7).

ConceptEncoders, decoders and multiplexers

CircuitInputs → outputsWhat it doesOne application
Encoder2n (or fewer) → ngives the binary code of the one active input linekeyboard → binary code; octal/decimal/hex to binary
Decodern → 2nactivates exactly the output line whose number is the input (each output is a minterm)memory address decoding; binary to hex/decimal display
Multiplexer (MUX)2n data + n select → 1routes the selected data input to the single outputsending many signals down one line (data selector); parallel to serial

Octal-to-binary encoder: A2 = D4 + D5 + D6 + D7, A1 = D2 + D3 + D6 + D7, A0 = D1 + D3 + D5 + D7 (three 4-input OR gates).

4 : 1 multiplexer: Y = S1′S0′I0 + S1′S0I1 + S1S0′I2 + S1S0I3.

Encoder: many → few. Decoder: few → many. MUX: many → one. A 2:4 decoder + 4 AND gates + 1 OR gate = 4:1 MUX.

ConceptMajority circuit

A three-input majority circuit outputs 1 when two or more inputs are 1 (a voting circuit). M(A,B,C) = Σ(3,5,6,7) = AB + BC + CA — the same function as a full adder’s CARRY. Overdue: named in the syllabus, never yet set on a board.

Majority = CARRY of a full adder = AB + BC + CA.

DerivationFull adder: SUM = A ⊕ B ⊕ C and CARRY = AB + BC + CA

Derive both from the canonical forms, and show CARRY = AB + C(A ⊕ B), the two-half-adder form.

Worked exampleQuick hardware one-markers

  • (a) A gate gives 1 for A=0,B=0 and 0 for A=1,B=0 and for A=1,B=1. Name it.
  • (b) The output of one NOR gate feeds both inputs of a second NOR gate. What single gate is this?
  • (c) A 4:1 MUX has S1S0 = 10. Which input reaches Y?
  • (d) Input D6 of an octal encoder is active. What is A2A1A0?
  • (e) How many gates, and of which kinds, make a full adder from two half adders? (Specimen 2025 Q1(x))
  • (f) Full adder inputs A=1, B=0, C=1: SUM and CARRY?
Show working
  • (a) NOR (XNOR would give 1 for A=1,B=1).
  • (b) ((A + B)′ + (A + B)′)′ = A + B: an OR gate.
  • (c) S1S0′ is true, so I2.
  • (d) 6 = 110 (A2 and A1 contain D6, A0 does not).
  • (e) 2 XOR, 2 AND, 1 OR — five gates.
  • (f) 1 + 0 + 1 = 102: SUM = 0, CARRY = 1.

Recall sheetRecall sheet

  • XOR = A′B + AB′ (inputs differ); XNOR = AB + A′B′ (inputs agree).
  • Half adder SUM = A ⊕ B, CARRY = AB. Full adder SUM = A ⊕ B ⊕ C = Σ(1,2,4,7), CARRY = AB + BC + CA = Σ(3,5,6,7).
  • Full adder = 2 half adders + OR: 2 XOR, 2 AND, 1 OR.
  • Encoder 2n → n (OR gates); decoder n → 2n (AND gates, one per minterm); MUX 2n + n select → 1.
  • NAND: NOT = (AA)′, AND = NAND then NOT, OR = NAND of inverted inputs. NOR: dual.
  • XOR needs 4 NAND or 5 NOR gates.
  • Majority circuit = AB + BC + CA.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Section A [5]: decoder (define + decode a given list of binary numbers to hex/decimal) or encoder (octal / decimal / hex to binary) — every board, rotating.
  • Section A [3]: full adder from two half adders; half vs full adder with SUM and CARRY (7 of 9 boards).
  • Section A [2–3]: build AND / OR / XOR using NAND only or NOR only, expression at each gate (7 of 9).
  • Section A [3 + 1]: logic diagram → derive (1), (2), X; reduce; name the gate (S24, S25, B25, B25I, B26).
  • Overdue: majority circuit truth table and expression; 4:1 MUX from a 2:4 decoder.

Units 4–9 · Java review: objects, types, expressions, statements, methods

Syllabus 4–9 (review of Class XI plus objects): objects and classes, constructors, Scanner and StringTokenizer, primitive types, wrapper classes, casting, operators and precedence, statements and scope, methods, primitive vs object arguments, static members, this. Examined as 2–3 one-mark Java items in Question 1, the 3-mark fill-in-the-code in Question 2(iv), and inside every Section B program.

ConceptObjects, classes and constructors

  • A class is a blueprint (a user-defined type) declaring data members (attributes) and methods (behaviour). An object is an instance of a class, created with new, which allocates it and calls a constructor.
  • A constructor has the class’s name and no return type (not even void); it initialises the data members. If a class declares none, Java supplies a default no-argument constructor. Constructors can be overloaded (default and parameterised) but are not inherited.
  • this refers to the current object: this.age = age; separates the data member from a parameter of the same name; this(...) calls another constructor.
  • static data members belong to the class (one copy shared by all objects); instance members belong to each object. A static method can use only static members directly and cannot use this or super.
  • static final declares a class constant: one copy, value fixed at initialisation.

Constructor: same name, no return type, called by new, not inherited.

FormulaePrimitive types and wrapper classes

TypeSizeRange / valuesWrapperString → value
byte1 byte−128 .. 127ByteByte.parseByte(s)
short2 bytes−32768 .. 32767ShortShort.parseShort(s)
int4 bytes−231 .. 231−1IntegerInteger.parseInt(s)
long8 bytes−263 .. 263−1LongLong.parseLong(s)
float4 bytes≈ 7 significant digitsFloatFloat.parseFloat(s)
double8 bytes≈ 15 significant digitsDoubleDouble.parseDouble(s)
char2 bytesUnicode '\u0000' .. '\uffff' (0 .. 65535)Characters.charAt(0)
boolean—true, falseBooleanBoolean.parseBoolean(s)
  • Autoboxing: Integer x = 5; wraps automatically; unboxing: int y = x;.
  • Wrapper classes live in java.lang, which is imported by default — no import needed.
  • Implicit widening (coercion): byte → short → int → long → float → double, and char → int. Narrowing needs an explicit cast: (int) 3.99 is 3 (truncates).
  • In an expression, byte, short and char are promoted to int: 'A' + 2 is the int 67.
  • Useful Character methods: isDigit, isLetter, isUpperCase, isLowerCase, isWhitespace, toUpperCase, toLowerCase.

parseXxx turns a String into a primitive; valueOf / toString go the other way.

ConceptOperators, precedence and evaluation

Precedence (high → low)OperatorsAssociativity
postfixa++ a--left to right
unary++a --a + - ! ~ (cast)right to left
multiplicative* / %left to right
additive+ -left to right
shift<< >> >>>left to right
relational< <= > >= instanceofleft to right
equality== !=left to right
logical&& then ||left to right
ternary? :right to left
assignment= += -= *= /= %=right to left
  • int / int is integer division (7 / 2 = 3); the sign of a % b follows a (−7 % 3 = −1).
  • a++ uses the value then increments; ++a increments then uses.
  • && and || short-circuit: the right operand is not evaluated when the left decides.
  • String + anything is concatenation, evaluated left to right: 1 + 2 + "3" is "33".
  • LHS of an assignment must be a variable (an l-value); the RHS is any expression of a compatible type.

Left to right for + : numbers add until the first String appears, then everything concatenates.

ConceptStatements, scope, methods and arguments

  • Conditionals: if, if-else, if-else-if ladder, switch (falls through to the next case without break), ternary ?:.
  • Loops: for, while (entry controlled), do-while (exit controlled, runs at least once); break leaves the loop, continue skips to the next iteration; return leaves the method (a void method may use bare return;).
  • Scope: a variable declared in a block (including a for header) exists only in that block.
  • Formal arguments are the parameters in the method header; actual arguments are the values passed in the call.
  • Java passes by value. For a primitive the value is copied, so the method cannot change the caller’s variable. For an object or array the reference is copied: the method can change the object’s contents, but reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller.
  • Input: Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in); nextInt, nextDouble, next (one token), nextLine (rest of line). A non-numeric token read by nextInt throws InputMismatchException. StringTokenizer (java.util) splits a String into tokens at whitespace or given delimiters: hasMoreTokens, nextToken, countTokens.

Primitive argument: copy of the value. Object argument: copy of the reference.

DiagramPrimitive vs object arguments in memory

DerivationWhy an int ranges from −231 to 231 − 1

Derive the range of an n-bit two’s-complement integer.

Show working
  1. n bits have 2n patterns. In two’s complement the leading bit has weight −2n−1 and the others +2n−2 … 20.
  2. Smallest: 1000…0 = −2n−1. Largest: 0111…1 = 2n−1 − 1.
  3. For int, n = 32: −2147483648 .. 2147483647. Adding 1 to the largest wraps round to the smallest.
int big = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
System.out.println(big + " " + Integer.MIN_VALUE);
System.out.println(big + 1);
2147483647 -2147483648
-2147483648

  • 'A' + 2 is int arithmetic: 65 + 2 = 67.
  • 'a' is 97; 97 − 32 = 65, cast to char: A.
  • 234 + 65 = 299 (Specimen 2022 Q16 type).
  • String + char concatenates: 234A.

Worked exampleOutput: increment, division, casting, concatenation

int a = 5;
int b = a++ + ++a;
System.out.println("b = " + b + ", a = " + a);
System.out.println(7 / 2 + " " + 7 / 2.0 + " " + (double)(7 / 2));
System.out.println((int) 3.99 + " " + (-7 % 3) + " " + (7 % -3));

Show working
b = 12, a = 7
3 3.5 3.0
3 -1 1
3345
-2 -2.0
  • a++ gives 5 (a becomes 6), then ++a gives 7: b = 12, a = 7.
  • (double)(7 / 2) divides first (3), then widens: 3.0.
  • The sign of % follows the dividend.
  • 1 + 2 = 3, then "3" joins: "33", then "334", "3345".
  • Math.round(x) = floor(x + 0.5): round(−2.5) = −2; ceil(−2.5) = −2.0 (a double).

Trap 7 / 2.0 is 3.5 but (double)(7 / 2) is 3.0 — the cast is applied to the already-truncated quotient.

Worked exampleOutput: switch fall-through, short-circuit and scope

int x = 2, i = 0;
String s = "";
switch (x)
{
    case 1: s += "one";
    case 2: s += "two";
    case 3: s += "three"; break;
    default: s += "none";
}
System.out.println(s);
if (i != 0 && 10 / i > 1)
    System.out.println("big");
else
    System.out.println("safe");
int k;
for (k = 1; k <= 10; k += 3) { }
System.out.println(k);
Show working
twothree
safe
13
  • Case 2 matches; with no break it falls into case 3, whose break stops it.
  • i != 0 is false, so 10 / i is never evaluated — no ArithmeticException.
  • k takes 1, 4, 7, 10, 13; the loop stops when k = 13 fails the test. (k is declared outside the loop, so it is in scope.)

Worked exampleOutput: primitive vs object arguments, static counter, this

class Demo
{
    static int count = 0;
    int id;
    Demo() { count++; this.id = count; }
    static void change(int n, int a[])
    {
        n = 10;
        a[0] = 10;
        a = new int[]{ 99 };
    }
    public static void main(String args[])
    {
        int x = 5;
        int arr[] = { 1, 2, 3 };
        change(x, arr);
        System.out.println(x + " " + arr[0]);
        Demo p = new Demo(), q = new Demo(), r = new Demo();
        System.out.println(q.id + " " + Demo.count + " " + p.count);
    }
}
Show working
5 10
2 3 3
  • x is copied: unchanged. arr’s reference is copied: a[0] = 10 changes the caller’s array; the later a = new int[]{99} only redirects the local copy.
  • count is static — one copy for the class, so p.count, q.count and Demo.count are all 3; q was the second object made.

Answer ?1? len / 2   ?2? len / 2   ?3? (a + b) * (a + b)

boolean isTech(int n)
{
    String s = String.valueOf(n);
    int len = s.length();
    if (len % 2 != 0)
        return false;
    int a = Integer.parseInt(s.substring(0, len / 2));
    int b = Integer.parseInt(s.substring(len / 2));
    return (a + b) * (a + b) == n;
}

Completed method, run on 2025, 3025, 1234, 123:

true true false false

Worked exampleStatements I, II, III (Question 1 pattern)

Given static final double PI = 3.142; in a class. I: PI has one copy shared by all objects. II: PI can be assigned a new value inside a method. III: static and final cannot be used together. Which are valid? (a) only I (b) I and II (c) II and III (d) only III. (Specimen 2025 Q1(viii), Board 2026 Q1(ii).)

Show working

Answer (a) only I. final forbids reassignment (compile error for II), and static final is the normal way to declare a class constant (III is false).

ProgramModel: a class with constructors, this and a static member

Class Account: data members accNo, balance, static count; default and parameterised constructors (using this); deposit(double), withdraw(double) that refuses an overdraft; display().

Show working
class Account
{
    static int count = 0;             // number of accounts opened
    int accNo;
    double balance;

    Account()                          // default constructor
    {
        this(0.0);                     // calls the parameterised one
    }
    Account(double balance)
    {
        count++;
        this.accNo = 1000 + count;
        this.balance = balance;        // this.balance is the data member
    }
    void deposit(double amt)
    {
        balance += amt;
    }
    boolean withdraw(double amt)
    {
        if (amt > balance)
            return false;              // no overdraft
        balance -= amt;
        return true;
    }
    void display()
    {
        System.out.println(accNo + " : " + balance);
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        Account a = new Account(500.0);
        Account b = new Account();
        a.deposit(250.0);
        System.out.println(b.withdraw(10.0));
        a.display();
        b.display();
        System.out.println("Accounts: " + Account.count);
    }
}

Output

false
1001 : 750.0

Accounts: 2

ProgramModel: StringTokenizer and wrapper conversion

Read a line of text, list its tokens and add the ones that are whole numbers (check with Character.isDigit, convert with Integer.parseInt).

Show working
import java.util.*;
class Tokens
{
    public static void main()
    {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
        String line = sc.nextLine();
        StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer(line, " ,");
        System.out.println("Tokens: " + st.countTokens());
        int sum = 0;
        while (st.hasMoreTokens())
        {
            String t = st.nextToken();
            boolean num = true;
            for (int i = 0; i < t.length(); i++)
                if (!Character.isDigit(t.charAt(i)))
                    num = false;
            if (num)
                sum += Integer.parseInt(t);
        }
        System.out.println("Sum of numbers = " + sum);
    }
}

Input

Marks 45, 67 and 8x plus 88

Output

Tokens: 7
Sum of numbers = 200

Recall sheetRecall sheet

  • Constructor: class name, no return type, invoked by new, overloadable, not inherited.
  • this = current object; static members: one copy per class; static methods cannot use this / super.
  • Sizes: byte 1, short 2, char 2, int 4, float 4, long 8, double 8 bytes.
  • parseInt / parseDouble: String → number; java.lang needs no import; autoboxing / unboxing.
  • Widening is automatic; narrowing needs a cast and truncates.
  • Integer division truncates; % takes the sign of the dividend; + goes left to right.
  • switch falls through without break; && and || short-circuit.
  • Java passes by value: a primitive copy, or a reference copy for objects and arrays.
  • Scanner: nextInt / next / nextLine; StringTokenizer: hasMoreTokens / nextToken / countTokens.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q1 Statements I/II/III MCQ on static final, this or extends / implements (S25, B25, B25I, B26).
  • Q1 VSA: relevance of static data members; purpose of this (B24 1(x), B23 1(viii)).
  • Q1 A–R on break / return / switch fall-through (B25 1(vi), B26 1(viii)).
  • Q2(iv) fill-in [1+1+1]: a special-number checker using String.valueOf / substring / parseInt, or a %10 /10 digit loop (5 papers since 2024).

Unit 10 · Arrays and strings

Syllabus 10: arrays (single and multi-dimensional), address calculation (row and column major), searching, maximum / minimum, sorting (bubble, selection, insertion), strings and the String class, StringBuffer. In the paper: Question 2(ii) address calculation [2] every year, and two of the three Section B programs (array / matrix with object passing; a String problem).

ConceptArrays and their storage

  • An array stores many values of one type under one name; a.length is its size; indices 0 .. length−1. Access is constant time: the address of any element is computed by a formula, independent of the number of elements.
  • int m[][] = new int[3][4]; is a 3-row, 4-column matrix; m.length = 3 rows, m[0].length = 4 columns. Rows may differ in length (jagged arrays).
  • Memory is one-dimensional, so a 2-D array is laid out either row by row (row-major) or column by column (column-major). (Java itself stores a 2-D array as an array of row arrays; the address questions assume one contiguous block, and ISC asks both orders.)

Constant-time access is why the address formula exists.

DiagramRow-major and column-major order

DerivationDeriving the address formulae

For A[Lr .. Ur][Lc .. Uc] with base address B (address of A[Lr][Lc]) and W bytes per element, M = Ur − Lr + 1 rows and N = Uc − Lc + 1 columns.

Show working
  1. Row-major: before row I come the complete rows Lr .. I−1, i.e. (I − Lr) rows of N elements. Within row I, J − Lc elements precede A[I][J].
  2. Elements before A[I][J] = N(I − Lr) + (J − Lc), each W bytes, so Address = B + W[N(I − Lr) + (J − Lc)].
  3. Column-major: (J − Lc) complete columns of M elements precede column J, then I − Lr elements within it: Address = B + W[(I − Lr) + M(J − Lc)].
  4. If the address given is of some other element A[i0][j0], use it as B with Lr = i0, Lc = j0 in the offsets (the count of elements between them is the same).

Trap Row-major multiplies by the number of columns N; column-major by the number of rows M. With negative lower bounds, I − Lr = I + |Lr|.

Worked exampleRow-major address (Board 2025 Q2(ii))

M[−1 .. 10][4 .. 13], W = 2 bytes, B = 1200, row-major. Find the address of M[2][7].

Show working
  1. Rows M = 10 − (-1) + 1 = 12; columns N = 13 − (4) + 1 = 10.
  2. Address of M[I][J] = B + W × [ N(I − Lr) + (J − Lc) ] (row-major order)
  3. Offset (in elements) = 10 × (2 − (-1)) + (7 − (4)) = 33
  4. Address = 1200 + 2 × 33 = 1266

Answer 1266

Worked exampleColumn-major address (Specimen 2025 = Board 2023 Q2(ii))

M[−6 .. 10][4 .. 15], W = 4 bytes, B = 1025, column-major. Find the address of M[4][8].

Show working
  1. Rows M = 10 − (-6) + 1 = 17; columns N = 15 − (4) + 1 = 12.
  2. Address of M[I][J] = B + W × [ (I − Lr) + M(J − Lc) ] (column-major order)
  3. Offset (in elements) = (4 − (-6)) + 17 × (8 − (4)) = 78
  4. Address = 1025 + 4 × 78 = 1337

Answer 1337

Worked exampleFind the base address (Board 2026 Q2(ii))

G[3 .. 7][2 .. 5] is stored column-major with W = 4 bytes; the address of G[5][4] is 6000. Find the base address.

Show working
  1. Rows M = 7 − (3) + 1 = 5; columns N = 5 − (2) + 1 = 4.
  2. Address of G[I][J] = B + W × [ (I − Lr) + M(J − Lc) ] (column-major order)
  3. Offset of G[5][4] from G[3][2] = (5 − (3)) + 5 × (4 − (2)) = 12
  4. 6000 = B + 4 × 12  ⇒  B = 6000 − 48 = 5952

Answer 5952

Worked exampleRow-major with negative bounds (Board 2024)

ARR[−5 .. 15][10 .. 20], W = 2, B = 2500, row-major. Find the address of ARR[10][15].

Show working
  1. Rows M = 15 − (-5) + 1 = 21; columns N = 20 − (10) + 1 = 11.
  2. Address of ARR[I][J] = B + W × [ N(I − Lr) + (J − Lc) ] (row-major order)
  3. Offset (in elements) = 11 × (10 − (-5)) + (15 − (10)) = 170
  4. Address = 2500 + 2 × 170 = 2840

Answer 2840

Worked exampleFind the element size W and the order m (Specimen 2020, Board 2018)

  • (a) arr[15][20], column-major: arr[1][1] is at 4000 and arr[6][8] at 4440. Find W.
  • (b) A[m][m], W = 4, column-major: A[1][1] at 1500, A[4][5] at 1608. Find m.
Show working
  1. (a) Elements from arr[1][1] to arr[6][8] (column-major, M = 15): (6 − 1) + 15(8 − 1) = 110. So 4440 = 4000 + 110W, W = 440 / 110 = 4 bytes.
  2. (b) Elements between: (1608 − 1500) / 4 = 27 = (4 − 1) + m(5 − 1) = 3 + 4m, so m = 6.

Note Both answers are checked by recomputing the second address from the first with the value found.

ConceptSearching and sorting

AlgorithmIdeaComparisons (worst)Best case
Linear searchcheck each element in turnn1 (first element)
Binary searchsorted array; compare with the middle, discard half⌊log2n⌋ + 11
Bubble sortcompare neighbours, swap if out of order; the largest bubbles to the end each passn(n−1)/2n−1 with an early-exit flag
Selection sortfind the smallest of the unsorted part, swap it to the frontn(n−1)/2n(n−1)/2 (always)
Insertion sorttake the next element and insert it into the sorted left part, shifting larger ones rightn(n−1)/2n−1 (already sorted)

Binary search needs a sorted array. Selection sort makes at most n−1 swaps.

Worked exampleTrace: insertion sort (descending) and bubble sort

Sort {5, 12, 7, 3, 8} into descending order by insertion sort, and {5, 1, 4, 2} into ascending order by bubble sort, showing the array after every pass.

Show working
class Traces
{
    static void show(int a[])
    {
        String s = "";
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)
            s += a[i] + " ";
        System.out.println(s.trim());
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        int a[] = { 5, 12, 7, 3, 8 };
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++)          // insertion, descending
        {
            int key = a[i], j = i - 1;
            while (j >= 0 && a[j] < key)
            {
                a[j + 1] = a[j];
                j--;
            }
            a[j + 1] = key;
            show(a);
        }
        int b[] = { 5, 1, 4, 2 };
        for (int i = 0; i < b.length - 1; i++)      // bubble, ascending
        {
            for (int j = 0; j < b.length - 1 - i; j++)
                if (b[j] > b[j + 1])
                {
                    int t = b[j]; b[j] = b[j + 1]; b[j + 1] = t;
                }
            show(b);
        }
    }
}

Output (four insertion passes, then three bubble passes):

12 5 7 3 8
12 7 5 3 8
12 7 5 3 8
12 8 7 5 3
1 4 2 5
1 2 4 5
1 2 4 5

Note Pass 3 of the insertion sort moves nothing: 3 is already smaller than everything to its left.

substring(a, b) takes a .. b−1 — length b − a.

Worked exampleOutput: String methods (Specimen 2022 Sem 2 type)

String a = "SUBMISSION", b = "Apple";
System.out.println(a.substring(3, 7));
System.out.println(a.indexOf('S', 3) + " " + a.lastIndexOf("S"));
System.out.println(b.compareTo("apple") + " " + "Cat".compareTo("Cattle"));
String t = a.toLowerCase();
a.toLowerCase();
System.out.println(a.charAt(0) + t.substring(8));
Show working
MISS
5 6
-32 -3
Son
  • substring(3, 7): indices 3..6 = MISS.
  • First 'S' at or after 3 is index 5; last 'S' is 6.
  • 'A' − 'a' = 65 − 97 = −32; when one string is a prefix of the other, compareTo gives the length difference 3 − 6 = −3.
  • a.toLowerCase() on its own changes nothing (immutability), so a.charAt(0) is still S; t.substring(8) is "on".

ProgramModel: an object returned by a method — TimeOp (Board 2026 Q6)

Class TimeOp: int arr[] holds hours, minutes, seconds. TimeOp(); void readTime(); TimeOp addTime(TimeOp tt) adds the times in tt and the current object, stores the result in a local object and returns it; void dispTime() prints h:m:s.

Show working
import java.util.*;
class TimeOp
{
    int arr[];
    static Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

    TimeOp()
    {
        arr = new int[3];                  // hours, minutes, seconds
    }
    void readTime()
    {
        System.out.println("Enter hours, minutes and seconds:");
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
            arr[i] = sc.nextInt();
    }
    TimeOp addTime(TimeOp tt)
    {
        TimeOp t = new TimeOp();            // local object for the result
        int s = this.arr[2] + tt.arr[2];
        int m = this.arr[1] + tt.arr[1] + s / 60;   // carry from seconds
        t.arr[2] = s % 60;
        t.arr[1] = m % 60;
        t.arr[0] = this.arr[0] + tt.arr[0] + m / 60; // carry from minutes
        return t;
    }
    void dispTime()
    {
        System.out.println(arr[0] + ":" + arr[1] + ":" + arr[2]);
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        TimeOp a = new TimeOp();
        TimeOp b = new TimeOp();
        a.readTime();
        b.readTime();
        TimeOp c = a.addTime(b);
        c.dispTime();
    }
}

Input

6 35 40
7 45 30

Output

14:21:10

Note One static Scanner for the class: a second Scanner on System.in may find the input already buffered by the first.

ProgramModel: two objects passed in — Colsum (Board 2025 Q7)

Class Colsum: int mat[][], m, n; Colsum(int mm, int nn); void readArray(); boolean check(Colsum A, Colsum B) returns true if every column of A has the same sum as the corresponding column of B; void print().

Show working
import java.util.*;
class Colsum
{
    int mat[][], m, n;
    static Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

    Colsum(int mm, int nn)
    {
        m = mm;
        n = nn;
        mat = new int[m][n];
    }
    void readArray()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++)
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
                mat[i][j] = sc.nextInt();
    }
    int colSum(int j)                      // sum of column j of this matrix
    {
        int s = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++)
            s += mat[i][j];
        return s;
    }
    boolean check(Colsum A, Colsum B)
    {
        if (A.n != B.n)
            return false;
        for (int j = 0; j < A.n; j++)
            if (A.colSum(j) != B.colSum(j))
                return false;
        return true;
    }
    void print()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++)
        {
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
                System.out.print(mat[i][j] + "\t");
            System.out.println();
        }
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        Colsum x = new Colsum(2, 3);
        Colsum y = new Colsum(3, 3);
        x.readArray();
        y.readArray();
        x.print();
        y.print();
        if (x.check(x, y))
            System.out.println("Both matrices have equal column sums");
        else
            System.out.println("Column sums are not equal");
    }
}

Input

1 2 3 4 5 6
1 1 1 2 3 4 2 3 4

Output

1	2	3	
4	5	6	
1	1	1	
2	3	4	
2	3	4	
Both matrices have equal column sums

ProgramModel: insertion sort in a class — InsSort (Board 2024 Q7)

Class InsSort: int arr[], size; InsSort(int s); void getArray(); void insertionSort() sorts in descending order; double find() returns the average of the odd elements; void display() prints the sorted array and the average.

Show working
import java.util.*;
class InsSort
{
    int arr[], size;
    static Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

    InsSort(int s)
    {
        size = s;
        arr = new int[size];
    }
    void getArray()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++)
            arr[i] = sc.nextInt();
    }
    void insertionSort()
    {
        for (int i = 1; i < size; i++)
        {
            int key = arr[i];
            int j = i - 1;
            while (j >= 0 && arr[j] < key)     // shift smaller elements right
            {
                arr[j + 1] = arr[j];
                j--;
            }
            arr[j + 1] = key;
        }
    }
    double find()
    {
        int sum = 0, c = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++)
            if (arr[i] % 2 != 0)
            {
                sum += arr[i];
                c++;
            }
        return c == 0 ? 0.0 : (double) sum / c;
    }
    void display()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++)
            System.out.print(arr[i] + " ");
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("Average of odd elements = " + find());
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        InsSort ob = new InsSort(6);
        ob.getArray();
        ob.insertionSort();
        ob.display();
    }
}

Input

5 12 7 3 8 9

Output

12 9 8 7 5 3
Average of odd elements = 6.0

ProgramModel: a String problem — StringOp mask removal (Specimen 2025 Q6)

Class StringOp: str, msk, nstr; void accept() reads both in lower case; void form() removes from str every character that occurs in msk, giving nstr; void display(). communication, mont → cuicai.

Show working
import java.util.*;
class StringOp
{
    String str, msk, nstr;
    static Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

    StringOp()
    {
        str = msk = nstr = "";
    }
    void accept()
    {
        System.out.println("Enter the string and the mask:");
        str = sc.next().toLowerCase();
        msk = sc.next().toLowerCase();
    }
    void form()
    {
        nstr = "";
        for (int i = 0; i < str.length(); i++)
        {
            char ch = str.charAt(i);
            if (msk.indexOf(ch) == -1)       // keep only characters absent from the mask
                nstr = nstr + ch;
        }
    }
    void display()
    {
        System.out.println("Original: " + str);
        System.out.println("Mask    : " + msk);
        System.out.println("Result  : " + nstr);
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        StringOp ob = new StringOp();
        ob.accept();
        ob.form();
        ob.display();
    }
}

Input

communication mont

Output

Original: communication
Mask    : mont
Result  : cuicai

ProgramModel: sorting the words of a sentence with StringTokenizer (Board 2023 SortAlpha type)

Read a sentence, split it into words with StringTokenizer, sort the words alphabetically (bubble sort using compareTo) and print them. THE SKY IS BLUE → BLUE IS SKY THE.

Show working
import java.util.*;
class SortWords
{
    public static void main()
    {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
        String sent = sc.nextLine().trim().toUpperCase();
        StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer(sent, " .?!");
        int n = st.countTokens();
        String w[] = new String[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            w[i] = st.nextToken();
        for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++)          // bubble sort
            for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++)
                if (w[j].compareTo(w[j + 1]) > 0)
                {
                    String t = w[j]; w[j] = w[j + 1]; w[j + 1] = t;
                }
        String out = "";
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            out += w[i] + " ";
        System.out.println(out.trim());
    }
}

Input

THE SKY IS BLUE.

Output

BLUE IS SKY THE

Recall sheetRecall sheet

  • Row-major: B + W[N(I − Lr) + (J − Lc)]. Column-major: B + W[(I − Lr) + M(J − Lc)].
  • M = Ur − Lr + 1 rows, N = Uc − Lc + 1 columns; a base given at an interior cell is used as the origin.
  • Bubble: neighbours swap. Selection: pick the minimum, one swap per pass. Insertion: shift and insert.
  • Binary search: sorted array, mid = (low + high) / 2, about log2n comparisons.
  • substring(a, b) excludes b; indexOf returns −1 if absent; compareTo returns a difference (or length difference).
  • String is immutable, StringBuffer mutable (append, insert, reverse, deleteCharAt, setCharAt).
  • Object passing: void f(X P, X Q) writes into this; X f(X P) builds a new X and returns it.
  • One static Scanner per class in a program that reads into several objects.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q2(ii) [2]: 2-D address, alternating row / column major, negative lower bounds; find the address, the base, W or the order (9 of 9 boards).
  • Section B slot 2 [10]: an array or matrix class with an object passed as argument or returned — TimeOp / Colsum / Mixarray / JoinArray patterns (8 of 9 boards).
  • Section B slot 3 [10]: a String / sentence class — mask removal, PendulumS, Flipgram, Palprime, vowel encoding (9 of 9).
  • A sort inside a class (insertion descending, bubble, selection) — set in 2024, and the syllabus names all three.
  • A–R on String immutability vs StringBuffer (S25 1(vii)).

Unit 11 · Recursion

Syllabus 11: concept of recursion, simple recursive methods (factorial, GCD, binary search, conversion between bases), the base case, Tower of Hanoi. In the paper: the Question 2(iii) dry run [2 + 1] every year, the recursive method inside Section B slot 1 [10] every year, and an A–R or VSA on recursion theory.

ConceptRecursion, base case and the call stack

  • A recursive method calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. It needs a base case that returns without recursing, and every recursive call must move towards it; otherwise the calls never end and the program fails with StackOverflowError.
  • Each call gets its own stack frame (parameters, local variables, return address). Calls are pushed (winding) until the base case, then popped in reverse order (unwinding), each returning its value to the caller.
  • Statements before the recursive call run on the way down; statements after it run on the way back up, in reverse order.
  • Direct recursion: f calls f. Indirect: f calls g, g calls f. Tail recursion: the recursive call is the last action.

Base case first; each call smaller; code after the call runs in reverse.

FormulaeRecursion vs iteration

RecursionIteration
Mechanismmethod calls itselfloop repeats a block
Terminationbase caseloop condition becomes false
Memoryone stack frame per active call — more memoryconstant extra memory
Speedslower (call overhead)faster
Codeshort and natural for self-similar problems (Hanoi, trees)can be long for such problems
FailureStackOverflowError if no base caseinfinite loop

Board 2026 Q7(ii) asked two differences between recursion and iteration [2].

DiagramCall stack of fact(4)

int fact(int n)
{
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1;              // base case
    return n * fact(n - 1);    // recursive case
}

DiagramRecursion tree of fib(4)

static int calls = 0;
int fib(int n)
{
    calls++;
    if (n <= 1)
        return n;
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

fib(4) = 3 after 9 calls. The number of calls grows roughly like 2n — the classic case where recursion is elegant but wasteful.

ConceptTower of Hanoi

Move n discs from peg A to peg C using B, one disc at a time, never placing a larger disc on a smaller. Recursive solution: move n−1 discs A → B (using C); move disc n A → C; move n−1 discs B → C (using A). Base case n = 0: do nothing. A non-recursive solution is far more complicated — the syllabus’s example of recursion’s elegance.

Moves for n discs: 2n − 1 (3 discs: 7 moves).

DerivationTower of Hanoi needs 2n − 1 moves

Let T(n) be the number of moves for n discs. Show T(n) = 2n − 1.

Show working
  1. From the method: T(0) = 0 and T(n) = T(n−1) + 1 + T(n−1) = 2T(n−1) + 1.
  2. Unroll: T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1 = 4T(n−2) + 2 + 1 = … = 2nT(0) + 2n−1 + … + 2 + 1.
  3. The geometric sum 1 + 2 + … + 2n−1 = 2n − 1, and T(0) = 0.
  4. Check by induction: T(0) = 0 = 20 − 1; if T(k) = 2k − 1 then T(k+1) = 2(2k − 1) + 1 = 2k+1 − 1.
class Hanoi
{
    static int moves = 0;
    static void move(int n, char from, char to, char via)
    {
        if (n == 0)
            return;                     // base case: nothing to move
        move(n - 1, from, via, to);     // clear the n-1 smaller discs
        moves++;
        System.out.println("Disc " + n + ": " + from + " -> " + to);
        move(n - 1, via, to, from);     // put them back on top
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        move(3, 'A', 'C', 'B');
        System.out.println("Total moves = " + moves);
    }
}
Disc 1: A -> C
Disc 2: A -> B
Disc 1: C -> B
Disc 3: A -> C
Disc 1: B -> A
Disc 2: B -> C
Disc 1: A -> C
Total moves = 7

DerivationWhy GCD by repeated subtraction is correct

Show gcd(a, b) = gcd(a − b, b) for a > b, which justifies the recursive method below.

Show working
  1. If d divides a and b, it divides a − b; so every common divisor of (a, b) is a common divisor of (a − b, b).
  2. Conversely if d divides a − b and b, it divides (a − b) + b = a.
  3. The two pairs have exactly the same common divisors, hence the same greatest one.
  4. Each step makes the larger number smaller while both stay positive, so the process reaches a = b, and gcd(a, a) = a (the base case).

Worked exampleDry run: base conversion workOut(220)

Board 2026 Q2(iii) pattern. The following function is a part of some class. Answer with the dry run: (a) the value returned (b) what the function computes apart from recursion.

String workOut(int n)
{
    if (n == 0)
        return "";
    int r = n % 16;
    char c = (r < 10) ? (char)('0' + r) : (char)('A' + r - 10);
    return workOut(n / 16) + c;
}

Unwinding: "" + "D" = "D", then "D" + "C" = "DC".

Answer (a) "DC". (b) It returns the hexadecimal form of n (decimal → hex by repeated division by 16).

int think(int a[], int f, int l)

int getIt(int x, int arr[], int f, int l)
{

        return -1;
    int m = (f + l) / 2;
    if (arr[m] == x)
        return m;
    else if (arr[m] < x)
        return getIt(x, arr, m + 1, l);
    else
        return getIt(x, arr, f, m - 1);
}

ProgramModel: Pernicious number with a recursive count (Board 2025 Q6)

Class Perni: int num (a binary number stored as an int); Perni(); void accept(); int countOne(int k) counts the 1s in k recursively; void check(): pernicious if it has at least two digits and the number of 1s is prime. 101 ✓, 10110 ✓, 1111 ✗.

Show working
import java.util.*;
class Perni
{
    int num;
    static Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

    Perni()
    {
        num = 0;
    }
    void accept()
    {
        System.out.println("Enter a binary number:");
        num = sc.nextInt();
    }
    int countOne(int k)
    {
        if (k == 0)
            return 0;                         // base case
        return (k % 10 == 1 ? 1 : 0) + countOne(k / 10);
    }
    boolean isPrime(int x)
    {
        if (x < 2)
            return false;
        for (int i = 2; i * i <= x; i++)
            if (x % i == 0)
                return false;
        return true;
    }
    void check()
    {
        int c = countOne(num);
        if (num >= 10 && isPrime(c))
            System.out.println(num + " is a Pernicious number");
        else
            System.out.println(num + " is not a Pernicious number");
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        Perni ob = new Perni();
        ob.accept();
        ob.check();
    }
}

Input

10110

Output

10110 is a Pernicious number

1111 gives “1111 is not a Pernicious number” (four 1s).

ProgramModel: recursive LCM (Specimen 2025 Q8, corrected)

Class LCM: n1, n2, large, sm, l; LCM(); void accept() reads n1, n2 and sets large and sm; int getLCM() finds the LCM recursively by stepping through the multiples of the larger number; void display().

Show working
import java.util.*;
class LCM
{
    int n1, n2, large, sm, l;
    static Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

    LCM()
    {
        n1 = n2 = large = sm = l = 0;
    }
    void accept()
    {
        System.out.println("Enter two numbers:");
        n1 = sc.nextInt();
        n2 = sc.nextInt();
        large = Math.max(n1, n2);
        sm = Math.min(n1, n2);
    }
    int getLCM()
    {
        if (large % sm == 0)                 // base case: a common multiple
            return large;
        large = large + Math.max(n1, n2);   // next multiple of the larger number
        return getLCM();
    }
    void display()
    {
        l = getLCM();
        System.out.println("LCM of " + n1 + " and " + n2 + " = " + l);
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        LCM ob = new LCM();
        ob.accept();
        ob.display();
    }
}

Input

12 18

Output

LCM of 12 and 18 = 36

Trap The printed Specimen 2025 key has no constructor although the question asks for one.

ProgramModel: recursive base conversion — the Evil number (Specimen 2024 Q6)

Class Evil: int num, String bin; void rec_bin(int x) builds the binary form of x in bin recursively; void check(): an Evil number has an even number of 1s in binary (10 = 1010 is Evil; 7 = 111 is not).

Show working
import java.util.*;
class Evil
{
    int num;
    String bin;

    Evil(int n)
    {
        num = n;
        bin = "";
    }
    void rec_bin(int x)
    {
        if (x > 0)
        {
            rec_bin(x / 2);                  // higher bits first
            bin = bin + (x % 2);             // then this bit, on the way back
        }
    }
    void check()
    {
        rec_bin(num);
        int c = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < bin.length(); i++)
            if (bin.charAt(i) == '1')
                c++;
        System.out.println(num + " = " + bin + " : " + (c % 2 == 0 ? "Evil" : "not Evil"));
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
        Evil ob = new Evil(sc.nextInt());
        ob.check();
    }
}

Input

10

Output

10 = 1010 : Evil

Input 7 gives 7 = 111 : not Evil.

Recall sheetRecall sheet

  • Every recursive method: base case (no recursion) + recursive case (a smaller problem).
  • Winding pushes frames; unwinding pops them in reverse; code after the call runs in reverse order.
  • No base case → StackOverflowError. Recursion uses more memory than iteration.
  • Hanoi: T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1 = 2n − 1 moves.
  • Recognise the dry runs: %16 / %8 / %2 then call on n/base → base conversion; f > l → array range; a−b → GCD; m − n, n + 2 → perfect square; n/2 → log2n.
  • Answer format: (a) the value with a call table; (b) one sentence naming what it computes.
  • Section B slot 1: data member(s), constructor, accept(), ONE recursive helper, a check / display, main().

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Q2(iii) [2 + 1] dry run: base conversion, recursion over an array range, recursive binary search (S25, not yet echoed), digit recursion, GCD (8 of 9 boards).
  • Section B slot 1 [10]: number class with a recursive method — Pernicious, Trimorphic, Evil / DeciHex, Dudeney, Mighty, recursive LCM (S25, not yet echoed), Armstrong (9 of 9).
  • Q2(iv) recursive fill-in (Armstrong sumOfPowers, S25).
  • A–R on recursion using more memory / the call stack (S25 1(ii), B24 1(vi)); recursion vs iteration [2] (B26 7(ii)).
  • Overdue: Tower of Hanoi (named in the syllabus, never set) — the number of moves, or the move order for 3 discs.

Unit 12 · Inheritance, interfaces and polymorphism

Syllabus 12: inheritance, super and derived classes, member access, redefinition of variables and methods, abstract classes, class Object, protected visibility, subclass polymorphism and dynamic binding; interfaces and their implementation. In the paper: Section C Question 10 [5] every year (write the subclass), and 1–2 one-mark items (interface, super / this, extends / implements, abstract, overloading).

ConceptInheritance, super and derived classes

  • class Sub extends Super: Sub (derived / child) inherits the non-private members of Super (base / parent). Use inheritance for a genuine is-a specialisation, not merely to reuse code.
  • Forms: single, multilevel (A → B → C, inheritance is transitive), hierarchical (one parent, many children). Java has no multiple inheritance of classes; a class may implement several interfaces.
  • Constructors are not inherited. The subclass constructor calls the superclass constructor with super(…), which must be its first statement; if omitted, super() is inserted, so the superclass constructors run first, top-down.
  • super.method() calls the superclass version of an overridden method; super.x reaches a hidden field.
  • Every class ultimately extends Object, which supplies toString(), equals(), hashCode().

super(...) first; members declared once in the superclass are used by name in the subclass.

FormulaeMember access

ModifierSame classSame packageSubclass (other package)Anywhere
privateyesnonono
(default)yesyesnono
protectedyesyesyesno
publicyesyesyesyes

A private member of the superclass is inherited in the object but not accessible by name in the subclass: declare it protected, or use the superclass’s public methods.

protected = package + subclasses.

ConceptOverriding, overloading, hiding and dynamic binding

OverloadingOverriding
Wheresame class (or inherited)subclass redefines a superclass method
Signaturesame name, different parameter listsame name, same parameters, same return type
Boundcompile time (static binding)run time (dynamic binding)
Polymorphismcompile-timerun-time / subclass polymorphism
  • A superclass reference may refer to a subclass object: Super s = new Sub();. A call s.show() runs Sub’s show() — the object’s class decides (dynamic binding).
  • Fields are not polymorphic: redeclaring a field in the subclass hides the superclass field, and s.x uses the reference’s type (see the diagram in the example below).
  • An abstract class cannot be instantiated; it may have abstract methods (no body) and ordinary ones. A concrete subclass must override every abstract method.
  • A final method cannot be overridden; a final class cannot be extended; static methods are hidden, not overridden.

Methods bind to the object, fields to the reference.

ConceptInterfaces

  • An interface declares method prototypes (implicitly public abstract) and constants (data members are implicitly public static final). A class implements it and must define every method.
  • A class may implement several interfaces, and extend a class at the same time: class Car extends Vehicle implements FourWheeler.
  • Purpose: to let the final user supply part of the implementation (e.g. the comparison in a general sort), to define a data structure as an abstract data type with several implementations, and to get multiple inheritance of type.
  • Since Java 8 an interface may also contain default and static methods with bodies.
  • The Java construct interface is not the same as the everyday word for a class’s set of public method prototypes.
Abstract classInterface
Methodsabstract and concreteabstract (plus default / static)
Dataany fieldsonly public static final constants
Inheritanceextends one classa class implements many
Constructoryesno

Interface data members are constants: public static final.

DiagramClass diagram: extends and implements (Board 2020 Q10)

DerivationWhy a superclass constructor always runs first

Show the order of constructor execution for new C() where C extends B extends A.

Show working
  1. The compiler makes super() (or the explicit super(…)) the first statement of every constructor.
  2. So C() first calls B(), whose first act is to call A(), whose first act is Object().
  3. The bodies therefore complete in the order Object, A, B, C: a subclass never sees an uninitialised superclass part.
class A { A() { System.out.print("A "); } }
class B extends A { B() { System.out.print("B "); } }
class C extends B { C() { super(); System.out.print("C"); } }
new C();
System.out.println();
A B C

Worked exampleOutput: dynamic binding and hidden fields

class P
{
    int x = 10;
    void show() { System.out.println("P " + x); }
}
class Q extends P
{
    int x = 20;
    void show() { System.out.println("Q " + x + " " + super.x); }
}
// in main:
P ob = new Q();
ob.show();
System.out.println(ob.x);
((Q) ob).show();
System.out.println(((Q) ob).x);
Show working
Q 20 10
10
Q 20 10
20
  • ob refers to a Q object, so ob.show() runs Q’s show() (dynamic binding).
  • ob.x uses the reference type P: 10. After the cast the reference type is Q: 20.

Worked exampleSpot the errors (competency booklet Q26–28 type)

class Shop
{
    private double price;
    Shop(double p) { price = p; }
}
class Sale extends Shop
{
    double disc;
    Sale(double p, double d)
    {
        disc = d;
        super(p);            // (1)
    }
    double net() { return price - disc; }   // (2)
}
Show working
  • (1) super(p) must be the first statement of the constructor.
  • (2) price is private in Shop, so Sale cannot use it by name: make it protected (or add a public getter in Shop).

Corrected, new Sale(500, 75).net() returns 425.0.

Worked exampleAssertion–Reason on interfaces and overloading

  • (i) A: A class implementing an interface cannot change the interface’s data members. R: Data members of an interface are implicitly public, static and final.
  • (ii) A: For overloaded methods the version called is decided at compile time. R: Overloaded methods differ in their parameter lists, which the compiler matches against the arguments of the call.
Show working
  • (i) (a) Both true, and R explains A: a final member cannot be reassigned by anyone.
  • (ii) (a) Both true, and R explains A: the compiler picks the version by matching the argument list.

ProgramModel: subclass with a slab charge — Library → Compute (after Specimen 2025 Q10)

Superclass Library: name, author, p (price), a parameterised constructor and show(). Subclass Compute: d (days kept), f (fine); constructor; void fine(): the first 7 days are free, then Rs 2 a day for the next 5 days, Rs 3 a day for the next 5, Rs 5 a day beyond that; void show() shows the book and the amount = 2% of the price per day kept + fine. The superclass and main( ) need NOT be written.

Show working

Given in the question (the superclass / class Node) not part of your answer

class Library
{
    protected String name, author;
    protected double p;                 // price of the book
    Library(String n, String a, double pr)
    {
        name = n;
        author = a;
        p = pr;
    }
    void show()
    {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name + "  Author: " + author + "  Price: " + p);
    }
}
class Compute extends Library
{
    int d;                              // days the book was kept
    double f;                           // fine

    Compute(String n, String a, double pr, int days)
    {
        super(n, a, pr);                // must be the first statement
        d = days;
        f = 0.0;
    }
    void fine()
    {
        int x = d - 7;                  // days beyond the allowed 7
        if (x <= 0)
            f = 0.0;
        else if (x <= 5)
            f = x * 2.0;
        else if (x <= 10)
            f = 5 * 2.0 + (x - 5) * 3.0;
        else
            f = 5 * 2.0 + 5 * 3.0 + (x - 10) * 5.0;
    }
    void show()
    {
        fine();
        super.show();
        double total = 0.02 * p * d + f;      // 2% of price per day + fine
        System.out.println("Days: " + d + "  Fine: " + f + "  Amount: " + total);
    }
}

For a Rs 500 book kept 20 days: 13 extra days = 5 × 2 + 5 × 3 + 3 × 5 = Rs 40; 2% × 500 × 20 = Rs 200; amount Rs 240.

Days: 20  Fine: 40.0  Amount: 240.0

interface Data
{

class CalVol extends Base implements Data

ProgramModel: abstract class and subclass polymorphism (syllabus 12(a), overdue)

An abstract class Shape with an abstract area(), two subclasses, and an array of Shape references whose show() calls pick the right area() at run time.

Show working
abstract class Shape
{
    String name;
    Shape(String n) { name = n; }
    abstract double area();             // no body
    void show() { System.out.println(name + " area = " + area()); }
}
class Circle extends Shape
{
    double r;
    Circle(double r) { super("Circle"); this.r = r; }
    double area() { return 3.14 * r * r; }
}
class Rect extends Shape
{
    double l, b;
    Rect(double l, double b) { super("Rect"); this.l = l; this.b = b; }
    double area() { return l * b; }
}
class Shapes
{
    public static void main()
    {
        Shape s[] = { new Circle(10.0), new Rect(4.0, 2.5) };
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length; i++)
            s[i].show();                // dynamic binding picks area()
    }
}
Circle area = 314.0
Rect area = 10.0

Recall sheetRecall sheet

  • extends: one superclass; implements: any number of interfaces; both together: extends first.
  • super(…) first in the constructor; super.show() inside the overriding show().
  • private not accessible in the subclass — protected is. Interface fields: public static final.
  • Overloading: same name, different parameters, compile time. Overriding: same signature, run time.
  • Superclass reference, subclass object: methods from the object, fields from the reference.
  • Abstract class: cannot be instantiated, may have constructors and concrete methods.
  • In the answer write only the subclass: no superclass, no main( ).

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Section C Q10 [5] every year: the subclass with super(…), a slab or formula computation and an overriding show() calling super.show() — billing / fine / surcharge / discount / overtime slabs (S25, B26, B24, B25I).
  • Overdue: an interface + class version (last set 2020) and an abstract class with dynamic binding (never set).
  • Q1: Statements I/II/III on extends / implements, A–R on interfaces with abstract and non-abstract methods (B26 1(vi)), one use of an interface (B24 1(vii)), keyword for multilevel inheritance, purpose of super.
  • Q1 A–R on overloading bound at compile time (B25I 1(ii)).

Unit 13 · Data structures

Syllabus 13: stack, queue, circular queue, dequeue implemented through classes and defined through an interface; infix to prefix and postfix; single linked list (insertion, deletion, reversal, extracting an element or a sublist, checking emptiness) by algorithm and program; binary trees and traversals (conceptual). In the paper: Question 2(i) conversion [2], Section C Q9 data-structure class [4 + 1] and Q11 linked list [2] + tree [3], every year.

ConceptStack, queue, circular queue and dequeue

StructurePrincipleOperationsEmpty / full (array of size cap)Applications
StackLIFOpush, pop, peek at topempty: top == −1; full: top == cap−1 (overflow / underflow)undo, browser back, recursion (call stack), expression conversion and evaluation
QueueFIFOinsert at rear, delete at frontempty: front == rear (or −1); full: rear == cap−1printer spooling, ticket counters, BFS
Circular queueFIFOas queue, indices advance modulo capfull: (rear+1) % cap == frontCPU round-robin scheduling, buffers; reuses freed front cells
Dequeueinsert / delete at both endspushfront, pushrear, popfront, poprearinput-restricted (insert one end) or output-restricted (delete one end)undo-redo, palindrome checking, work stealing

A data structure is best defined as an abstract data type: a Java interface listing the operations, with one or more classes implementing it (array-based, linked).

Stack LIFO at top; queue FIFO rear-in front-out; circular queue wraps with % cap; dequeue both ends.

ProgramModel: circular queue — CirQueue (Board 2025 Q9, Board 2020 Q10)

int Q[], cap, front, rear; CirQueue(int max); void push(int v) adds at the rear, or prints QUEUE IS FULL; int pop() removes from the front, or returns −999 if empty. (ii) One application: CPU round-robin scheduling.

Show working
class CirQueue
{
    int Q[], cap, front, rear;
    CirQueue(int max)
    {
        cap = max;
        Q = new int[cap];
        front = rear = -1;             // empty
    }
    void push(int v)
    {
        if ((rear + 1) % cap == front)
            System.out.println("QUEUE IS FULL");
        else
        {
            if (front == -1)
                front = 0;
            rear = (rear + 1) % cap;   // wrap round
            Q[rear] = v;
        }
    }
    int pop()
    {
        if (front == -1)
            return -999;               // empty
        int v = Q[front];
        if (front == rear)
            front = rear = -1;         // queue has become empty
        else
            front = (front + 1) % cap;
        return v;
    }
}

Test: push 10..60 into cap 5, pop twice, push 60 and 70, then empty it:

QUEUE IS FULL
10 20
front=2 rear=1

ProgramModel: dequeue — ReCycle (Specimen 2025 Q9, corrected; not yet echoed by a board)

int ele[], cap, front, rear; ReCycle(int max); void pushfront(int v), void pushrear(int v) with “full from front / rear” messages; int popfront(), int poprear() returning −999 when empty. (ii) Name the entity: a dequeue (double-ended queue) — insertion and deletion at both ends; it is not FIFO.

Show working
class ReCycle
{
    int ele[], cap, front, rear;       // elements occupy ele[front .. rear-1]
    ReCycle(int max)
    {
        cap = max;
        ele = new int[cap];
        front = rear = 0;
    }
    void pushfront(int v)
    {
        if (front == 0)
            System.out.println("full from front");
        else
            ele[--front] = v;
    }
    void pushrear(int v)
    {
        if (rear == cap)
            System.out.println("full from rear");
        else
            ele[rear++] = v;
    }
    int popfront()
    {
        if (front == rear)
            return -999;               // empty
        return ele[front++];
    }
    int poprear()
    {
        if (front == rear)
            return -999;
        return ele[--rear];
    }
}
full from front
10
30
5 20 -999

Trap The printed Specimen 2025 key uses q[] for ele[], writes q[front--] and returns q[rear--] (post-decrement, so pushfront overwrites the current front element and poprear returns the unused cell at rear), and calls the principle FIFO. A dequeue is neither FIFO nor LIFO.

ProgramModel: stack — Browser history (Board 2026 Q9)

String pages[], max, top; Browser(int m); void visit(String url) pushes or reports full; String back() pops the latest page. (ii) Entity: stack, principle LIFO.

Show working
class Browser
{
    String pages[];
    int max, top;
    Browser(int m)
    {
        max = m;
        pages = new String[max];
        top = -1;
    }
    void visit(String url)             // push
    {
        if (top == max - 1)
            System.out.println("Browser history full");
        else
            pages[++top] = url;
    }
    String back()                      // pop
    {
        if (top == -1)
            return "No previous browser history";
        return pages[top--];
    }
}

b.com, a.com, No previous browser history

ProgramModel: a stack defined through an interface, two implementations (syllabus 13(a), overdue)

Interface IStack (push, pop, isEmpty) implemented by an array-based and a linked class; the same client code works with either, through an IStack reference.

Show working
interface IStack                       // the abstract data type
{
    void push(int v);
    int pop();                         // -9999 when empty
    boolean isEmpty();
}
class ArrayStack implements IStack
{
    int a[], top = -1;
    ArrayStack(int n) { a = new int[n]; }
    public void push(int v)
    {
        if (top == a.length - 1) System.out.println("OVERFLOW");
        else a[++top] = v;
    }
    public int pop() { return top == -1 ? -9999 : a[top--]; }
    public boolean isEmpty() { return top == -1; }
}
class LinkedStack implements IStack
{
    class Cell { int v; Cell next; Cell(int x, Cell n) { v = x; next = n; } }
    Cell top = null;
    public void push(int v) { top = new Cell(v, top); }   // never full
    public int pop()
    {
        if (top == null) return -9999;
        int v = top.v;
        top = top.next;
        return v;
    }
    public boolean isEmpty() { return top == null; }
}
OVERFLOW
33 22 11
44 33 22 11

Note The array version of capacity 3 overflows on the fourth push; the linked version never fills.

ConceptInfix, prefix and postfix

  • Infix A + B (operator between); prefix / Polish + A B (operator before); postfix / reverse Polish A B + (operator after). Prefix and postfix need no brackets and no precedence rules, which is why a stack machine evaluates them easily.
  • Precedence: ^ (right-associative) > * / % > + −; equal precedence is left-associative.
  • Postfix algorithm: scan left to right; operand → output; ( → push; ) → pop to the matching (; operator → pop while the top has higher or equal precedence (only higher for ^), then push; at the end pop all.
  • Prefix: bracket fully in order of evaluation and move each operator in front of its operands; or reverse the infix (swapping brackets), convert, and reverse the result — but in that reversed scan an operator pops only operators of strictly higher precedence (and does pop an equal ^). With the postfix rule unchanged, A − B − C would come out as −A−BC, which is A − (B − C); the right answer is −−ABC.
  • Evaluate postfix with a stack: push operands; on an operator pop two (the first popped is the right operand) and push the result.

Postfix: operands keep their order; only operators move.

Work inside out: bracket every operation in the order it is done, then write each operator before its two operands.

  1. Fully bracket by precedence: ((P/Q)+((S*F)+(X/R)))

  3. (S*F) → *SF
  4. (X/R) → /XR

  6. ((P/Q)+((S*F)+(X/R))) → +/PQ+*SF/XR

The same answer with a stack: reverse the infix (swapping the brackets), convert it as for postfix but pop only on strictly higher precedence (for ^, higher or equal), then reverse the output.

ConceptSingle linked list

  • A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding data and a reference (link) to the next node; start refers to the first node and the last node’s link is null. The node class is self-referential (a field of its own type).
  • Unlike an array it grows and shrinks at run time and inserts / deletes without shifting, but has no direct access: reaching the k-th node takes k steps.
  • Traversal pattern: Node t = start; while (t != null) { … t = t.next; } — the test is t != null, not t.next != null, or the last node is skipped.

The node class used below (printed in the question) not part of your answer

class Node
{
    int data;
    Node next;
    Node(int d)
    {
        data = d;
        next = null;
    }
}

Empty list: start == null. Loop on t != null.

ProgramLinked list: count the nodes with odd data (Board 2017; Board 2025 Imp. countNodes type)

int countOdd(Node start) returns the number of nodes whose data is odd. Write an Algorithm OR a Method.

Show working

Algorithm

Step 1. Start
Step 2. Set temp = start, c = 0
Step 3. Repeat steps 4 to 5 while temp != null
Step 4.   If temp.data is odd then c = c + 1
Step 5.   temp = temp.next
Step 6. Return c
Step 7. End

Method

int countOdd(Node start)
{
    int c = 0;
    Node t = start;
    while (t != null)
    {
        if (t.data % 2 != 0)
            c++;
        t = t.next;
    }
    return c;
}

On 12 → 7 → 30 → 5 it returns 2.

ProgramLinked list: search for a value (Specimen 2025 FindNode, corrected)

void findNode(Node start, int b) prints the position of b or “not found”. Write an Algorithm OR a Method.

Show working

Algorithm

Step 1. Start
Step 2. Set temp = start, pos = 1
Step 3. Repeat steps 4 to 5 while temp != null
Step 4.   If temp.data == b then print "found at", pos and go to step 7
Step 5.   temp = temp.next, pos = pos + 1
Step 6. Print "not found"
Step 7. End

Method

void findNode(Node start, int b)
{
    Node t = start;
    int pos = 1;
    while (t != null)              // tests the last node too
    {
        if (t.data == b)
        {
            System.out.println(b + " found at node " + pos);
            return;
        }
        t = t.next;
        pos++;
    }
    System.out.println(b + " not found");
}

Trap The printed Specimen 2025 key loops while temp.link != null and so never tests the last node.

ProgramLinked list: insert at the beginning and at the end (Specimen 2023, Board 2023)

Node insertBeg(Node start, int v) and Node insertEnd(Node start, int v) return the (new) start. Write an Algorithm OR a Method.

Show working

Algorithm

insertBeg:
Step 1. Create node n with data v
Step 2. n.next = start
Step 3. start = n; return start
insertEnd:
Step 1. Create node n with data v and next = null
Step 2. If start == null then return n
Step 3. temp = start; while temp.next != null, temp = temp.next
Step 4. temp.next = n; return start

Method

Node insertBeg(Node start, int v)
{
    Node n = new Node(v);
    n.next = start;
    return n;                      // new start
}
Node insertEnd(Node start, int v)
{
    Node n = new Node(v);
    if (start == null)
        return n;
    Node t = start;
    while (t.next != null)
        t = t.next;
    t.next = n;
    return start;
}

ProgramLinked list: delete a node (syllabus; never yet set on a board)

Node delete(Node start, int v) removes the first node holding v and returns the start. Write an Algorithm OR a Method.

Show working

Algorithm

Step 1. If start == null then return null
Step 2. If start.data == v then return start.next
Step 3. temp = start
Step 4. While temp.next != null and temp.next.data != v, temp = temp.next
Step 5. If temp.next != null then temp.next = temp.next.next
Step 6. Return start

Method

Node delete(Node start, int v)
{
    if (start == null)
        return null;
    if (start.data == v)
        return start.next;         // deleting the first node
    Node t = start;
    while (t.next != null && t.next.data != v)
        t = t.next;
    if (t.next != null)
        t.next = t.next.next;      // bypass the node
    return start;
}

9 → 12 → 7 → 30 → 5 with delete(7) becomes 9 → 12 → 30 → 5.

ProgramLinked list: reverse the list; check emptiness; extract a sublist (syllabus)

Node reverse(Node start), boolean isEmpty(Node start), Node sublist(Node start, int a, int b). Write an Algorithm OR a Method.

Show working

Algorithm

reverse:
Step 1. prev = null, cur = start
Step 2. While cur != null: nx = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = nx
Step 3. Return prev (the new start)
isEmpty: return start == null
sublist: walk with a position counter; copy each node whose position lies in a..b to a new list

Method

Node reverse(Node start)
{
    Node prev = null, cur = start;
    while (cur != null)
    {
        Node nx = cur.next;
        cur.next = prev;           // turn the link round
        prev = cur;
        cur = nx;
    }
    return prev;
}
boolean isEmpty(Node start)
{
    return start == null;
}
Node sublist(Node start, int a, int b)     // copy of nodes a..b (1-based)
{
    Node head = null, tail = null, t = start;
    for (int pos = 1; t != null && pos <= b; pos++, t = t.next)
        if (pos >= a)
        {
            Node n = new Node(t.data);
            if (head == null) head = n; else tail.next = n;
            tail = n;
        }
    return head;
}

All eight methods were run together: build 12, 7, 30, 5; count odd = 2; find 5 at node 4; insert 9 at the front; delete 7 and 9; sublist(2, 3) = 30 → 5; reverse = 5 → 30 → 12.
