Note Some books count height and depth in nodes rather than edges (one more). State the convention you use; ISC questions usually say which (Board 2026: “when the root is at level 0”).

Leaf: no children. Level: from the root down. Height: to the deepest leaf.

ConceptTraversals and the binary search tree

  • Preorder (NLR): node, left subtree, right subtree — T: A B D E H C F G I.
  • Inorder (LNR): left, node, right — T: D B H E A C G F I.
  • Postorder (LRN): left, right, node — T: D H E B G I F C A.
  • The root is first in preorder and last in postorder; in inorder it separates the left and right subtrees.
  • In a binary search tree every left descendant is smaller and every right descendant larger than the node, so inorder gives ascending order (competency Q19).

Pre: root first. Post: root last. In: root in the middle; BST inorder is sorted.

DerivationCounting nodes in a binary tree

Prove: (a) level l has at most 2l nodes; (b) a tree of height h has at most 2h+1 − 1 nodes; (c) in any non-empty binary tree, leaves n0 = n2 + 1, where n2 is the number of nodes with two children.

Show working
  1. (a) Induction: level 0 has 1 = 20 node. Each node at level l has at most 2 children, so level l+1 has at most 2 · 2l = 2l+1.
  2. (b) Sum over levels 0..h: 1 + 2 + … + 2h = 2h+1 − 1. Equality holds for a perfect tree.
  3. (c) Let n = n0 + n1 + n2. Every node except the root has exactly one incoming edge, so edges = n − 1. Counting outgoing edges, edges = n1 + 2n2. Hence n0 + n1 + n2 − 1 = n1 + 2n2, i.e. n0 = n2 + 1.
  4. Check on T: leaves D, H, G, I (4); two-child nodes A, B, F (3): 4 = 3 + 1. The BST: 4 leaves, 3 two-child nodes, 7 = 23 − 1 nodes at height 2.

Recall sheetRecall sheet

  • Stack LIFO (top = −1 empty); queue FIFO; circular queue full when (rear + 1) % cap == front; dequeue at both ends.
  • Q9 answer: only the methods asked, inside class X { }; messages and −999 exactly as specified; (ii) name + principle.
  • Postfix: operands in order; pop ≥ precedence (only > for ^); ) pops to (.
  • Prefix: bracket, then move each operator to the front; check with the root operator = last one evaluated.
  • Postfix evaluation: the first value popped is the right operand.
  • Linked list loop: while (t != null). Insert at front: n.next = start; start = n. Delete: prev.next = prev.next.next.
  • Reverse: prev = null; loop {nx = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = nx}.
  • Pre NLR, In LNR, Post LRN. Level from root (0). n0 = n2 + 1; at most 2h+1 − 1 nodes.

Unit 14 · Complexity and Big O notation

Syllabus 14: concrete computational complexity, input size, dominant term, constants, best / average / worst case, Big O notation, complexity of searching and sorting. In the paper: one Question 1 item every year, and in 2024 a 2-mark Q11(i).

ConceptComplexity and Big O

  • Input size n measures the problem (elements to sort, digits of a number). Complexity counts the basic operations (comparisons, assignments) as a function of n, independent of the machine.
  • Big O: f(n) is O(g(n)) if f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for some constant c and all n ≥ n0 — an upper bound on growth.
  • Dominant term: only the fastest-growing term matters; constants and lower terms are dropped: 3n2 + 5n + 7 is O(n2).
  • Best, average, worst case: the least, typical and most work over inputs of size n. Linear search: best 1 (first element), worst n (last or absent), average about n/2 — all O(n) except the best case O(1).
  • Rules: sequential blocks add (keep the larger); nested loops multiply; a loop that halves or doubles its variable is O(log n).
ClassNameTypical code
O(1)constanta fixed number of statements; array access by index
O(log n)logarithmicbinary search; a loop with i = i / 2 or i = i * 2
O(n)linearone loop over the data; linear search
O(n log n)linearithmica loop of n around a halving loop
O(n2)quadratictwo nested loops; bubble, selection, insertion sort
O(2n)exponentialnaive recursive Fibonacci, Tower of Hanoi

Drop constants, keep the dominant term; nested multiply, sequential add.

Selection sort is n2 even on sorted input; insertion sort is then n.

DerivationThe triangular loop is O(n2)

for (i = 1; i ≤ n; i++) for (j = 1; j ≤ i; j++) … (Board 2026 Q1(v)). Count the inner executions.

Show working
  1. For each i the inner body runs i times, so the total is 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2.
  2. n(n+1)/2 = n2/2 + n/2; the dominant term is n2/2 and the constant ½ is dropped.
  3. Hence O(n2). The same sum, n(n − 1)/2, counts the comparisons of bubble, selection and insertion sort in the worst case.

DerivationBinary search is O(log n)

Show that binary search makes at most ⌊log2n⌋ + 1 comparisons.

Show working
  1. Each comparison halves the part still to be searched: n, n/2, n/4, … elements.
  2. After k comparisons at most n/2k elements remain; the search must stop when this drops below 1, i.e. after k > log2n steps.
  3. So the worst case is ⌊log2n⌋ + 1 comparisons: O(log n). For n = 1000 that is 10, against 1000 for linear search.

DerivationDropping constants: 3n2 + 5n + 7 is O(n2)

Find c and n0 in the definition.

Show working
  1. For n ≥ 1: 5n ≤ 5n2 and 7 ≤ 7n2.
  2. So 3n2 + 5n + 7 ≤ 3n2 + 5n2 + 7n2 = 15n2: c = 15, n0 = 1.
  3. No constant c makes it ≤ c·n for all n, so it is not O(n): n2 is the dominant term (Board 2024 Q11(i) asked for it).

ProgramModel: count comparisons of linear and binary search

Search a sorted array of n = 1000 elements for a missing value with both methods and count the comparisons.

Show working
class Compare
{
    static int lin = 0, bin = 0;
    static int linear(int a[], int x)
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)
        {
            lin++;
            if (a[i] == x)
                return i;
        }
        return -1;
    }
    static int binary(int a[], int x)
    {
        int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
        while (lo <= hi)
        {
            int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
            bin++;
            if (a[mid] == x)
                return mid;
            if (a[mid] < x)
                lo = mid + 1;
            else
                hi = mid - 1;
        }
        return -1;
    }
    public static void main()
    {
        int a[] = new int[1000];
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)
            a[i] = 2 * i;                    // sorted, all even
        linear(a, 2001);
        binary(a, 2001);
        System.out.println("linear: " + lin + "  binary: " + bin);
    }
}
linear: 1000  binary: 10

Worst case: n against ⌊log21000⌋ + 1 = 10.

Worked exampleOne-markers on complexity

  • (a) Differentiate O(n) and O(n2) with an example of each (Specimen 2025 Q1(ix)).
  • (b) Four println statements, against a loop that prints four times: complexity of each? (competency Q42)
  • (c) Best and worst case of bubble sort with a swapped flag (Board 2020).
  • (d) Which is the dominant term of 2n3 + 100n2 + 5000?
Show working
  • (a) O(n): work grows in proportion to n — a single loop, linear search. O(n2): grows with the square — nested loops, bubble sort.
  • (b) Both O(1): the number of steps is fixed and does not depend on any input size.
  • (c) Best O(n): already sorted, one pass with no swap ends it. Worst O(n2): reverse order.
  • (d) 2n3; the complexity is O(n3).

Recall sheetRecall sheet

  • Big O = upper bound on growth; drop constants and lower terms.
  • Nested loops multiply, sequential loops add, halving / doubling is log n.
  • Triangular nested loop: n(n+1)/2 = O(n2).
  • Linear search O(n), binary O(log n); bubble / selection / insertion O(n2); selection is n2 even in the best case.
  • Best / average / worst: least / typical / most work for inputs of size n.
  • Hanoi and naive Fibonacci are exponential.
